stops.name: Tlaxcala: the regroup, and the sickness that does what the sword could not
stops.campa: Tlaxcala takes in the broken army again without demanding tribute for it, burying the Spanish dead and nursing the wounded through a summer of recovery and recrimination. Some captains want to sail for Cuba and be done with it, and Cortés holds the alliance together by will and by the promise of Tenochtitlan's gold still owed. Meanwhile a Narváez sailor's smallpox, carried unnoticed into the valley months before, is doing what no Spanish weapon yet has: it burns through a population with no resistance to it, killing the new emperor Cuitláhuac within eighty days of his taking the throne, and emptying whole cities before the siege guns are even cast.

stops.name: Texcoco, the thirteen brigantines built
stops.campa: At allied Texcoco on the lake's eastern shore, Cortés makes his winter headquarters and sets the shipwright Martín López to cutting timber in the Tlaxcalan hills for thirteen flat-bottomed brigantines, their planking and rigging hauled overland piece by piece by thousands of Tlaxcalteca porters and assembled on the shore in a canal dug for the launching. It is a siege engine no army of this hemisphere has ever seen: warships that will out-range and outgun every war-canoe on the lake, giving a land force command of the water that surrounds and feeds the city it means to starve.

stops.name: Tenochtitlan: the siege begins, the aqueduct cut
stops.campa: The brigantines launch onto Texcoco lake and clear it of war-canoes within the first engagements; on land, three armies under Alvarado, Sandoval, and Olid, Spaniards and tens of thousands of native allies who have waited a generation for this, advance down the great causeways while the freshwater aqueduct from Chapultepec is cut at its source. Tenochtitlan, an island city that has always drawn its life from the water around it, is walled off from food, from drinking water, and from escape all at once. What follows will be recorded as the longest and cruelest siege the Mexica have ever fought.

stops.name: Tlatelolco, the last stand and the taking of Cuauhtémoc
stops.campa: Street by street, canal by canal, the city is fought down to its last market square at Tlatelolco, where Cuauhtémoc, young nephew of Moctezuma, tlatoani since Cuitláhuac's death of the smallpox, has held the resistance for eighty days on famine rations of lizards and lake-scum, refusing every offer of terms. On the day of San Hipólito his canoe, fleeing across the lake with what treasure remains, is run down by the brigantine of García Holguín. Brought before Cortés, he lays a hand on the captain's own dagger and asks to be killed outright rather than live a captive emperor. Cortés spares him, for now, and Tenochtitlan falls silent.
stops.quote: que ya él había hecho todo lo que de su parte era obligado para defenderse a sí y a los suyos hasta venir a aquel estado, que ahora hiciese de él lo que yo quisiese; y puso la mano en un puñal que yo tenía, diciéndome que le diese de puñaladas y le matase.
stops.quote_source: Hernán Cortés, Tercera Carta de Relación a Carlos V (15 de mayo de 1522)

stops.name: Coyoacán: the burned feet, the gold never found
stops.campa: At his headquarters in Coyoacán, on the lake's southern shore, Cortés presses Cuauhtémoc and the lord of Tacuba for the treasure the soldiers swear vanished into the canals on the Noche Triste: the famous gold of Moctezuma that Spain never sees whole again. Tradition, though not Cortés's own account, holds that their feet are burned with oil to make them speak, and that they name a lake few divers ever search successfully. Cuauhtémoc endures it as he has endured everything since the canoe was taken, and gives up little the Spaniards did not already suspect was gone for good.

stops.name: Mexico City, the new capital rises on the ruins
stops.campa: Over the broken temples and canals of Tenochtitlan, Cortés lays out a Spanish city on the old Aztec grid, using the same causeways, the same central island, even much of the same stone: the Great Temple's own carved blocks go into the walls of the new cathedral and the viceregal palace. Tens of thousands of native laborers, the empire's own former subjects, do the building under the old system of forced labor now serving new masters. Within a few years a lake-city that took the Mexica two centuries to raise is a Spanish capital again, and the name Tenochtitlan survives mostly in the mouths of the conquered.

stops.name: Coatzacoalco, departure for Las Hibueras
stops.campa: Restless as governor, jealous of any captain who might carve out a rival kingdom, Cortés sets out from his own town of Espíritu Santo on the Coatzacoalco river with a great retinue, falconers, jugglers, a portable chapel, herds of pigs, and Cuauhtémoc himself brought along as a hostage against rebellion, to punish his lieutenant Cristóbal de Olid, gone rogue in Honduras. The march becomes a two-year ordeal through unmapped jungle, the Chontal country of Acalan, and the flooded lowlands toward the Petén, a folly of pride that will cost him, by the time it ends, the very governorship he set out to protect.

stops.name: Izancanac, Cuauhtémoc hanged
stops.campa: In the Chontal Maya town of Izancanac on the Candelaria river, worn down by hunger, mutinous soldiers, and a report, never proven, never quite disproven, that Cuauhtémoc and the lord of Tacuba plot an uprising against the column, Cortés has both men seized in the night and hanged from a ceiba tree without formal trial. Cuauhtémoc meets it, the chroniclers agree, with the same composure he showed at his capture, naming the betrayal for what it is before he dies. The empire's last free tlatoani is buried far from his lake, fourteen hundred miles into a jungle that swallows the exact place.
stops.quote: ¡Oh, Malinche, días hacía que yo tenía entendido que esta muerte me habías de dar y había conocido tus falsas palabras, porque me matas sin justicia! Dios te la demande, pues yo no me la di cuando a ti me entregué en mi ciudad de México.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 177

stops.name: Trujillo, Honduras: the death-march's end
stops.campa: The column that reaches Trujillo on the Honduran coast is a wreck of the army that left Coatzacoalco: dead of hunger, dead of fever, some who deserted into the forest and were never found. Olid is already dead by another hand before Cortés even arrives; the expedition's whole purpose is spent before it is achieved. Word reaches him here that in his long absence rivals in Mexico City have seized the governorship, spread rumor of his own death, and begun dividing his estate. He will spend a year more finding his way home by sea to a capital that no longer expects him.

stops.name: Toledo, audience with Charles V
stops.campa: Vindicated by a royal investigation that clears him of the worst charges laid by his enemies, Cortés sails for Spain in 1528 to plead his case in person, bringing native jugglers, animals, gold and feather-work that dazzle the whole court, and Charles V receives him at Toledo with honor: the Order of Santiago, the rank of captain-general restored, audiences and favor after years of being libeled in his absence. It is the peak of his standing with the crown he has served; every honor after this comes slower, and every return to New Spain finds his authority a little more hedged about by royal caution.

stops.name: Béjar, marriage to Juana de Zúñiga
stops.campa: At the ducal town of Béjar, Cortés marries Doña Juana de Zúñiga, niece of the Duke of Béjar and daughter of the Count of Aguilar: a match into the high nobility of Castile no conquistador's fortune could have bought him ten years before. She will bear him the legitimate son, Martín, who inherits the marquisate, and cross the ocean with him afterward along with his aged mother, Catalina Pizarro, who dies within months of reaching the country her son conquered. The marriage seals what the crown's honors have already begun: the wool-merchant's grandson made, at last, a Spanish grandee.

stops.name: The Marquesado del Valle de Oaxaca granted
stops.campa: By royal cédula Charles V creates Cortés Marqués del Valle de Oaxaca, with twenty-three thousand vassals in perpetuity and civil and criminal jurisdiction over a domain larger than most Spanish kingdoms: lands scattered through Oaxaca, Morelos, Veracruz, and the Valley of Mexico itself. It is the largest private grant the crown has ever made in the Indies, and it outlives him: the title and its lands pass down through five generations of descendants, disputed, reduced, litigated over for three centuries, but never fully extinguished, the one piece of the empire he took that the crown could not simply confiscate.
